transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Title: Security Review - Observability & Audit Logs (Redwood Private)
Date/Time: 2025-02-06 18:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Naomi Feldman, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Colin O'Donnell
NorthBridge Health Systems: Janet Miller (CISO), Raj Patel (Security Engineering), Emily Chen (GRC), Tom Alvarez (Platform)

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, we’re at the top of the hour. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the security review focused on observability and audit logs for Redwood Private. Janet, Raj, Emily, Tom — good to meet.

[00:12] Janet Miller: Yep, thanks. We’re trying to close out our go-live checklist for the pilot, and audit logging is one of the bigger gaps right now.

[00:20] Liam O'Rourke: Totally. I’ve got Naomi from security/compliance product, Marcus from security engineering, Kevin who owns audit export/SIEM integration on our side, and Colin for customer integrations. We can do quick intros and then go straight into your questions.

[00:33] Naomi Feldman: Hi everyone. I help define what we consider “supported” for Private deployments from a security posture—defaults, logging, evidence.

[00:40] Marcus Lin: Hey. I’m on the security engineering team. Mostly RBAC, auth, and hardening around these components.

[00:46] Kevin Osei: Hi. I work on audit log export patterns and SIEM forwarding guidance, including field schemas and redaction.

[00:52] Colin O'Donnell: Colin here, I cover identity/network/logging integrations for Private installs.

[00:58] Raj Patel: Great. Raj, security engineering.

[01:00] Emily Chen: Emily, compliance. I’m the person who asks annoying questions about evidence.

[01:04] Tom Alvarez: Tom, platform. I’ll be the one actually wiring up Prometheus and Grafana on our side.

[01:10] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. Janet, do you want to frame what you need from this call?

[01:15] Janet Miller: Sure. We have three buckets. One is: what audit logs exist out of the box if we deploy your “minimum pack” dashboards and alerts. Two is: access control—can we enforce SSO, RBAC, and get logs for who accessed what. And three is: retention and immutability. We’re healthcare, so we have internal policy plus… not exactly HIPAA for everything, but we treat it like that.

[01:41] Liam O'Rourke: Makes sense. Maybe Naomi, can you level-set what the observability min pack includes and where the boundary is?

[01:48] Naomi Feldman: Yeah. So the “minimum pack” is not a new backend. It’s a bundle: Grafana dashboards, Prometheus alert rules, and log pipeline defaults. In Private, you can run it in a couple ways: customer-managed Grafana/Prometheus (most common in regulated), or in some cases we deploy a reference stack inside the cluster if that’s acceptable.

[02:10] Naomi Feldman: Either way, audit logging and retention—those are typically controlled by the customer’s observability stack and SIEM, but we provide guidance and we standardize the signals so you can produce evidence.

[02:23] Emily Chen: When you say “signals,” do you mean application logs, or like… access logs too?

[02:27] Kevin Osei: Both. There are a few categories: (1) Redwood service logs (gateway, runtime, control plane components) with structured fields; (2) metrics and alerts (Prometheus); and (3) audit logs for administrative actions, which for the observability tools usually means Grafana audit logs + API logs, and the Kubernetes audit logs for changes to ConfigMaps/Secrets/PrometheusRule resources.

[02:52] Raj Patel: Okay, that’s actually one of my key questions. Grafana: can we tell who changed a dashboard, who changed a data source, who viewed a dashboard? We need that for our internal change control.

[03:04] Marcus Lin: Yes, with some caveats depending on how you run Grafana. Grafana has “server” logs and an audit logging feature in enterprise, but even OSS can emit logs for login events and API calls depending on config. The cleanest pattern we recommend is:
- Use SSO (SAML or OIDC) so user identity is consistent.
- Disable anonymous access.
- Restrict “Editor/Admin” roles.
- Turn on request logging / API logs.
- Forward Grafana logs to your SIEM.

[03:35] Tom Alvarez: We run Grafana Enterprise already, so we can do the audit logs on our side.

[03:39] Marcus Lin: Great, that makes it easier. Then you can get explicit events for dashboard create/update/delete, folder permission changes, data source changes, and login events.

[03:52] Emily Chen: And do you have a mapping of which events we should collect as evidence? Like, “these are the minimum ones to be compliant with your supported criteria.”

[04:01] Naomi Feldman: We do. It’s in our security guidance doc for the pack. It’s basically: auth events, privilege changes, dashboard/rule changes, and data export configuration changes. We’ll send that after the call. It’s not a full compliance framework, but it maps to common SOC 2 type controls.

[04:20] Janet Miller: Prometheus rule changes. How do we audit those? Because our worry is someone changes alert thresholds and we don’t know.

[04:28] Kevin Osei: Right. Prometheus itself doesn’t always give you a nice “user changed rule X” audit event, because in Kubernetes it’s often a CRD like PrometheusRule. The recommended audit source is the Kubernetes audit log: it records who changed which object, from which IP, via which credential.

[04:47] Raj Patel: That means we have to enable kube-apiserver audit logging. We do have that in our platform cluster. But if your installer or charts modify those CRDs, we want to see those changes as well.

[04:58] Colin O'Donnell: Yep, and you’ll see them. The installer typically uses a dedicated service account. So your audit logs will show something like “system:serviceaccount:redwood:installer” or similar, depending on namespace, and the verb (create/update/patch) on PrometheusRule, ConfigMap, etc.

[05:17] Tom Alvarez: Just to confirm, you’re not like… making changes from outside the cluster. It’s all in-cluster controller applying YAML.

[05:23] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. For air-gapped and for Private in general, we assume minimal external dependencies. The operator/installer applies manifests. No outbound call to Redwood for this part unless you explicitly allow it for update checks.

[05:39] Janet Miller: That’s good. Another question: your own components—gateway, runtime—do they have audit logs, like for config changes? Or is it just service logs?

[05:50] Kevin Osei: Today, it’s a combination. We have structured logs for key events, including auth failures, policy eval decisions, and config reloads. For “who changed config,” again the source of truth is typically Kubernetes audit logs (ConfigMap/Secret updates) and GitOps logs if you use Argo/Flux.

[06:10] Naomi Feldman: We’re also adding “installer health” and some lightweight “who did what” events on the control plane side, but for Private the expectation is: your change-management system plus Kubernetes audit log is your evidence trail.

[06:26] Emily Chen: Let me ask it more bluntly. If an auditor asks “show me the log where Raj changed the alert threshold,” what do we show?

[06:34] Marcus Lin: You show the Kubernetes audit log event: user Raj’s identity from your IdP (or their kube credential), the API request patching the PrometheusRule object, timestamp, and the object name/namespace. You can also show the Git PR and merge record if you do GitOps. Grafana dashboards are similar: Grafana audit logs for changes if you manage dashboards in UI; or GitOps history if you provision dashboards from config.

[07:03] Raj Patel: Okay. That’s workable.

[07:06] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we should cover retention and “immutability,” because that tends to drive architecture.

[07:12] Janet Miller: Yes. We need at least 365 days for security audit logs. For system/application logs we do 90 days hot, and longer in archive depending on the system. Can your pack store that?

[07:26] Naomi Feldman: The pack itself doesn’t store logs long term. We ship defaults for collecting and forwarding. Retention is controlled by your logging backend—Splunk, Elastic, object storage, etc.

[07:39] Tom Alvarez: We’re a Splunk shop. We use HEC and also some syslog in older areas.

[07:44] Kevin Osei: Great. We have patterns for Splunk HEC. We can emit JSON logs and forward via Fluent Bit or Vector. The defaults are usually “structured JSON in, minimal parsing,” and then field extractions on Splunk side.

[08:01] Raj Patel: Do you support Vector? We’ve standardized on Vector.

[08:05] Kevin Osei: Yes, we generally recommend Vector for on-prem because it’s easier to control buffering and backpressure. Fluent Bit is also supported. The minimum pack will include suggested configs for both—filters, sampling, redaction.

[08:22] Emily Chen: Sampling? That worries me.

[08:24] Kevin Osei: Totally fair. Sampling is for high-volume request logs, not for security-relevant events. The guidance is: don’t sample auth failures, admin actions, or error logs above a certain severity. You might sample “successful request access logs” if volume is huge and you’re cost constrained, but we can set defaults conservative.

[08:47] Janet Miller: We probably want no sampling for audit logs, and maybe limited sampling for access logs, but only after we’re stable.

[08:55] Kevin Osei: That aligns with what we usually do.

[09:00] Raj Patel: What exactly is in your structured logs? Are there request IDs? User IDs? Tenant? Model? Also we need redaction because prompts can contain PHI.

[09:10] Kevin Osei: Yes. So the structured fields include request_id, tenant_id (or workspace), route, model, status_code, error_code, and latency breakdowns. For identity, in Private it depends on whether you pass end-user identity to Redwood. Many customers keep end-user identity outside and treat Redwood as a service identity. If you do pass a user claim, we recommend hashing or pseudonymizing.

[09:38] Marcus Lin: On redaction: we strongly recommend not logging prompts/responses by default in Private. The pack is designed so dashboards don’t require any content logs. If you choose to log payloads for debugging, that should be explicit, time-bounded, and protected.

[09:56] Tom Alvarez: That’s good. We want “no content logs” by default.

[10:00] Emily Chen: But then how do we do forensic analysis if there’s an incident?

[10:04] Marcus Lin: You can still do forensic analysis on metadata: who called what endpoint, when, what model, how many tokens, error codes, and trace IDs. If you need payload, we’d recommend a separate controlled pipeline with strong access control. Not baseline.

[10:23] Janet Miller: Another compliance point: evidence that dashboard access is controlled. Like, who can view “production performance dashboard.”

[10:31] Marcus Lin: That’s Grafana permissions. Folder-based permissions with roles. If you use SSO groups, you map groups to Grafana teams/roles. Audit logs show access and permission changes.

[10:48] Raj Patel: Do you support SAML for Grafana in the reference stack you install? Or is that on us?

[10:54] Colin O'Donnell: In customer-managed Grafana, it’s on you. In a Redwood-provisioned Grafana (if you choose that), we can configure OIDC/SAML depending on your IdP and whether you allow the necessary connectors. But for regulated, we usually recommend you bring your own Grafana and we just provision dashboards.

[11:16] Liam O'Rourke: I want to underline that: the “minimum pack” is compatible with customer-managed Grafana/Prometheus. It’s not “Redwood runs your Grafana.”

[11:27] Janet Miller: Okay.

[11:28] Emily Chen: Can we talk about “evidence for compliance” from Redwood? Do you provide any attestation that your components generate certain logs? Like a list of required fields?

[11:39] Naomi Feldman: We do. We have a “minimum signals standard” internally that lists metric names and required log fields/labels—like route/model labels, request IDs, error codes. The pack references that contract. We can share the relevant sections.

[12:00] Emily Chen: Great. Also, do you have SOC 2?

[12:03] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. For Private, of course, some controls move to you, but we can share our report under NDA.

[12:12] Janet Miller: Good.

[12:14] Raj Patel: I’ve got a more technical one. Prometheus and Grafana logs might be separate, but what about the log forwarder itself? If Vector is down or dropping events, we need an alert.

[12:26] Kevin Osei: Yes. The min pack includes “pipeline health” alerts: backlog, drops, export failures, and a “missing signals” group that fires if expected metrics/logs stop arriving. It’s basically: if collector output errors spike, or if log volume goes to zero for a component that’s known to be live.

[12:50] Tom Alvarez: How do you detect “logs volume is zero”? Prometheus can’t see logs.

[12:55] Kevin Osei: Right—there are two approaches. One is: the collector exports internal metrics (Vector metrics endpoint) into Prometheus. Those include counts of events processed, dropped, bytes sent, etc. Then you alert on those. The other is using your log backend queries (Splunk) which is out-of-band. We focus on the first for the baseline.

[13:21] Raj Patel: Okay. As long as there’s something.

[13:25] Emily Chen: On data retention: you said you don’t store it. But do any of your components store logs locally on disk that could violate retention policies?

[13:34] Marcus Lin: By default, the containers write to stdout/stderr, which the node logging agent collects. There isn’t a built-in long-term store. For buffering, Vector might buffer on disk depending on config. That’s configurable. Our guidance is: bounded buffer with encryption at rest if you do disk buffering, and keep the node volume protected.

[13:58] Tom Alvarez: We have encrypted node volumes. Fine.

[14:02] Janet Miller: We also have a “no egress” requirement in some environments. Can we still do updates, and can you still provide support if logs can’t leave?

[14:12] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. Air-gapped mode is supported for the pack. Updates are through offline bundles (container images and helm charts) that you mirror internally. For support, you can export logs and metrics snapshots manually—like sanitized bundles.

[14:30] Raj Patel: You said “sanitized.” Do you have a tool for that?

[14:33] Colin O'Donnell: The installer includes a “support bundle” command in most Private installs. It collects diagnostics—component status, versions, recent logs—optionally redacted. For observability specifically, we also have a validation command that checks dashboards load, rules parse, endpoints reachable.

[14:55] Naomi Feldman: And just to be clear, we design the min pack so support can do day-1 triage without needing content payload logs.

[15:06] Emily Chen: We’ll need to review what’s in that support bundle. Our policy is strict.

[15:10] Liam O'Rourke: Absolutely. We can send a sample manifest of what it collects.

[15:16] Janet Miller: Back to audit logs. For Redwood’s own control plane in Private—policy changes, routing rules, model version pinning—are those logged?

[15:26] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy/routing changes are logged as control plane events. The detail depends on the version you deploy, but in general you’ll get: who initiated the change (service identity), what object changed (policy name), and timestamps. If you integrate with your IdP, we can tie actions to user identities in the admin UI. If you manage via GitOps, again, you’ll have Git history.

[15:54] Raj Patel: Is the admin UI even in scope for the min pack? Or are we talking just dashboards.

[15:58] Naomi Feldman: The min pack is observability. But since you asked, the Private control plane has its own logs and audit events. We’re aligning the two so operators can see “routing fallback behavior,” “auth integration health,” and have evidence when changes occur.

[16:17] Tom Alvarez: The “fallback behavior” dashboards—those are metrics only, right?

[16:20] Naomi Feldman: Exactly. Metrics like fallback_count, route_decision_count, maybe region failover events. No payload.

[16:33] Emily Chen: One more compliance thing: time synchronization. Audit logs are useless if clocks drift.

[16:39] Marcus Lin: Agree. We require NTP (or your time sync standard) on cluster nodes. And for components, we use node time. We call that out in prerequisites.

[16:52] Janet Miller: Okay.

[16:54] Raj Patel: Can you talk about encryption? Like in transit and at rest for logs, especially if buffered.

[17:01] Colin O'Donnell: In transit: we recommend TLS from collectors to SIEM endpoints. For Splunk HEC, that’s standard TLS with token auth. At rest: it’s your storage system—Splunk indexers, object storage with encryption, and for any on-node buffers, encrypted volumes.

[17:21] Kevin Osei: Also, we avoid putting secrets in dashboards. Tokens (like Splunk HEC tokens) are stored in Kubernetes Secrets; access controlled via RBAC.

[17:33] Raj Patel: About secrets: will any dashboards show tokens in “data source config”? Grafana can leak those.

[17:39] Marcus Lin: Good catch. For Grafana, we recommend restricting who can view data source settings. Viewers should not have data source admin. Also, provisioning via files can keep secrets out of UI. In Grafana Enterprise you can also lock down.

[17:59] Tom Alvarez: We already do that.

[18:02] Emily Chen: Do you have a recommended separation of duties? Like, who can edit dashboards versus who can edit alert rules.

[18:09] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Typically: Platform/SRE has rights to manage alert rules and folders. App teams might get viewer access and maybe limited editor in non-prod only. We’ll share a recommended RBAC matrix.

[18:28] Janet Miller: Okay. Now, question about evidence: do you provide any “report” out of the installer that says “audit logging is enabled” and “minimum signals present.”

[18:38] Colin O'Donnell: The installer validation can output a report showing: Prometheus rules loaded, Grafana reachable, dashboards provisioned, metrics endpoints scraped. For “audit logging enabled,” we can verify some configs for Grafana if it’s the one we install; for customer-managed Grafana, we can provide a checklist but we can’t introspect everything unless you allow.

[19:06] Raj Patel: That’s fine. We just need a checklist we can sign.

[19:10] Emily Chen: With references. Like, “here’s the control, here’s the configuration, here’s where to find the log.”

[19:16] Naomi Feldman: Yep. That’s exactly what the audit logging considerations doc looks like.

[19:23] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s drill into one thing: “who viewed what.” Some orgs treat dashboard views as audit events, some don’t. Janet, do you need that?

[19:33] Janet Miller: For privileged dashboards, yes. At minimum for admin console and for anything that might expose sensitive operational data.

[19:42] Marcus Lin: Grafana can log logins and sometimes dashboard access depending on configuration/plugins. Grafana Enterprise has more explicit audit events. If you already have it, you should be able to get those.

[19:56] Tom Alvarez: We can.

[19:57] Raj Patel: For Prometheus UI, we usually disable it for most users anyway.

[20:01] Marcus Lin: That’s also our recommendation. Treat Prometheus as backend-only, query via Grafana with RBAC.

[20:10] Emily Chen: What about alert acknowledgements? If an alert is silenced, we need to know who did it.

[20:16] Kevin Osei: That’s Alertmanager. Alertmanager has API logs and can be integrated with auth in front of it. If you use Grafana Alerting, it also has audit events. In Kubernetes, we often put an auth proxy in front of Alertmanager. But again, the min pack provides rules; the alerting backend is yours. We can recommend patterns.

[20:41] Raj Patel: We use Alertmanager, with an OAuth proxy.

[20:44] Kevin Osei: Good. Then your proxy logs plus Alertmanager logs can show silence creation.

[20:52] Janet Miller: We’re getting into a lot of “it depends.” That’s okay, but we need something concrete to take to our compliance board.

[20:59] Naomi Feldman: Understood. The concrete piece is: we define the minimum set of audit-relevant events and where they live (Grafana audit logs, Kubernetes audit logs, collector metrics/logs, control plane events). Then we give a reference configuration and a validation checklist.

[21:19] Emily Chen: Do you have any customers in healthcare doing this already?

[21:24] Liam O'Rourke: We do, but I can’t name them on this call. We can provide a generalized architecture and we can also do a reference call under mutual NDA later.

[21:34] Janet Miller: Okay.

[21:36] Raj Patel: Another question: does Redwood generate any audit events for “model was changed” or “deployment changed”?

[21:43] Kevin Osei: For model version changes and routing policies, yes. Those are control plane logs. In Private, those logs can be forwarded like any other component logs.

[21:58] Tom Alvarez: Are those logs structured? Like JSON.

[22:01] Kevin Osei: Yes, JSON. We’re standardizing fields across gateway/runtime/control plane: timestamp, component, request_id where applicable, event_type, tenant/workspace, and an error_code if any.

[22:19] Emily Chen: Do you support OpenTelemetry?

[22:22] Caleb Johnson: (crosstalk) Sorry, Caleb isn’t on—

[22:24] Liam O'Rourke: Yeah we don’t have Caleb on this one. But yes, we do support OpenTelemetry for traces/metrics in the platform. For the minimum pack, we’re mostly Prometheus metrics + logs. Tracing is optional.

[22:40] Raj Patel: If we enable tracing, does it include payload?

[22:44] Marcus Lin: No, not by default. Traces have spans with attributes—route, latency, status. You control what attributes are included.

[22:55] Janet Miller: Okay.

[22:58] Emily Chen: Now about “immutability.” Our auditors sometimes ask for WORM storage. Can you support that?

[23:05] Kevin Osei: We don’t provide a WORM system directly. But the standard pattern is: forward audit logs to Splunk (which can be configured for retention and controls), and/or archive to object storage with WORM policies (S3 Object Lock, if you use AWS; or equivalent on-prem). We can recommend how to route the relevant logs.

[23:29] Raj Patel: Do you sign logs? Like cryptographic signing.

[23:33] Marcus Lin: Redwood services don’t cryptographically sign each log line today. Integrity is typically guaranteed by your logging pipeline controls and storage immutability. If log signing is a hard requirement, we should capture that as a requirement and see what’s acceptable—some customers rely on WORM storage + access controls.

[23:56] Janet Miller: It may not be hard requirement, but I need to check.

[23:59] Emily Chen: For SOC 2, WORM isn’t required, but for our internal policy we like it for security logs.

[24:06] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s add that as an open item. Janet, you can confirm your policy, and we’ll propose the recommended architecture.

[24:16] Tom Alvarez: Also, does your log schema include client IP? We sometimes need that.

[24:22] Kevin Osei: Gateway logs can include source IP, but in Kubernetes it might be the load balancer IP unless you preserve X-Forwarded-For. We can include the header-derived client IP if you trust that header from your ingress.

[24:43] Raj Patel: We do, we terminate at our ingress.

[24:45] Kevin Osei: Then yes, we can.

[24:49] Emily Chen: What about “who called the inference endpoint.” Is that captured?

[24:53] Marcus Lin: It depends if you use end-user auth through Redwood or you authenticate upstream and call Redwood with a service token. Many customers do service-to-service only. If you want per-user attribution, you’d need to include a user claim or header and we’d log it in a privacy-preserving way.

[25:14] Janet Miller: For now, service identity is fine.

[25:17] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Another thing that comes up: can dashboards themselves leak sensitive data? Naomi mentioned no secrets.

[25:25] Naomi Feldman: Yep. Dashboards show metrics like RPS, latency percentiles, error rates, GPU utilization, queue depth, cache hit rates. No request content. Variables include things like model name and route. We also put guardrails on cardinality so you don’t blow up Prometheus.

[25:48] Raj Patel: Cardinality… we had that happen with another vendor.

[25:52] Naomi Feldman: Yeah. We cap labels and we advise against labels like request_id in metrics. request_id stays in logs/traces.

[26:04] Tom Alvarez: Good.

[26:06] Emily Chen: On audit logs: do you log failed login attempts to the Redwood admin UI/control plane?

[26:13] Marcus Lin: Yes, auth failures are logged. For the UI, if it’s behind your IdP, you also get IdP logs which are actually better evidence.

[26:25] Janet Miller: We use Okta.

[26:26] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Then Okta system logs + Grafana audit logs + Kubernetes audit logs gives you a pretty complete picture.

[26:38] Raj Patel: Provided we wire it all.

[26:40] Liam O'Rourke: And that’s why we’re doing the “minimum pack,” so it’s less bespoke.

[26:45] Tom Alvarez: Quick question: are the dashboards provisioned via ConfigMaps?

[26:50] Naomi Feldman: Usually yes, via Grafana provisioning config. So changes can be managed in Git, and Kubernetes audit log records changes.

[27:02] Emily Chen: That’s actually good for evidence.

[27:05] Raj Patel: But if someone edits dashboards in UI, won’t that drift?

[27:10] Marcus Lin: Yes. We recommend disabling UI edits in prod by restricting editor roles, or using a “provisioned dashboards are read-only” mode. Grafana supports that behavior.

[27:25] Tom Alvarez: We can enforce that.

[27:28] Janet Miller: Okay, I think we’re close. I just want to make sure: the baseline includes guidance for Grafana audit logs, and “minimum signals.” But if we bring our own Grafana, Redwood won’t configure it.

[27:41] Naomi Feldman: Correct. We provide dashboards and reference configs; you operate Grafana. We’ll tell you what settings must be enabled to be “supported.”

[27:53] Emily Chen: That “supported” word—can you define it? Like, if we don’t have audit logs enabled, are we unsupported?

[28:00] Naomi Feldman: For Private, “supported” means: Redwood can reasonably help diagnose issues using the baseline signals. If audit logging is required by your policy, we’ll recommend it strongly, but lack of Grafana audit logs won’t necessarily block support for performance issues. However, for certain security incidents, if there’s no audit trail, we can’t help reconstruct. We can phrase it as “required for regulated/security posture” versus “required for operational support.”

[28:32] Janet Miller: That distinction helps.

[28:34] Raj Patel: Can you send that in writing.

[28:36] Liam O'Rourke: Yes.

[28:38] Tom Alvarez: I also want to ask about data residency. If we forward logs to Splunk Cloud, that’s our choice. You’re not sending anything to Redwood, right?

[28:48] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. In air-gapped, there is zero telemetry out unless you explicitly set it up. In VPC mode, you can also choose “no egress.”

[29:02] Emily Chen: Are there any calls home for license checks.

[29:05] Colin O'Donnell: No for the min pack. For some enterprise features there can be a license file, but not online checks. We’ll confirm based on the SKU.

[29:17] Janet Miller: Good.

[29:19] Raj Patel: One more: do you log admin actions in the Redwood installer itself? Like “installed version X,” “rolled back,” “changed flags.”

[29:29] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, installer logs include install/upgrade events, versions, and failure reasons. Those logs can be forwarded like any other. There are also metrics for installer health that drive a dashboard.
